summary: This document describes a way for DNS operators to update DNSSEC delegation trust information using the DNS itself as the communication channel. It targets cases where moving key information from a child zone to its parent is currently hard, such as when rolling Key Signing Keys.

eli5.summary: When a child gets a new house key, the parent needs a copy. This RFC lets the child leave a note in the DNS so the parent can find the new key without lots of paperwork.

subtitle: Two DNS record types that let a signed child zone tell its parent which DS records it wants.

tldr.problem: Every time a DNS operator changes the key that its parent zone represents in a DS record, the new key information has to reach the parent, often by a manual process that is easy to get wrong or to skip.
tldr.mechanism: The child zone publishes CDS and CDNSKEY records at its apex that state what its DS set should look like. The parent's agent polls for them, checks them against fixed acceptance rules, and updates the DS records.
tldr.outcome: Key rollovers can be automated, and a third-party DNS provider can maintain DNSSEC keys without receiving the registrant's registrar credentials. The RFC is Informational and has been updated by RFC 8078, RFC 9615 and RFC 9975.

today: RFC 7344 is an Informational RFC published in September 2014. It has been updated by RFC 8078, RFC 9615 and RFC 9975, and has not been obsoleted, so read those updates alongside it.

sections.title: The Problem with Updating Delegation Keys
sections.content:
The first time a DNS operator signs a zone, it must give its keying material to the parent through some out-of-band method to complete the chain of trust. Depending on the parent, the child might send its DNSKEY record, a DS record, or both. Each later key change must also be communicated to the parent and published in the parent's zone, and for each key change there may be up to two interactions with the parent.

The RFC says this is often a manual process, and any manual process is susceptible to mistakes. Because it is annoying, operators may avoid changing keys or skip needed steps. The proposal is to use the DNS itself: since DNSSEC provides data integrity for what is published, DNS publication can automate maintenance of delegation information. The document automates only the publication of DS records after the first one is in place. It does not cover NS and glue records, which a separate protocol, CPSYNC-DNS, is meant to handle.
sections.eli5: Telling the parent about a new key usually means filling in forms by hand, and people make mistakes or put it off. This RFC lets the DNS carry the message instead.

sections.title: Parents, Children and Operators
sections.content:
The Child is the entity that holds the delegation of a domain from the Parent, the domain in which the child is registered. The Child DNS Operator maintains and publishes the child's zone, and the Parental Agent is the entity the child deals with to change its delegation information. The parent holds a DS RRset that describes the DNSKEYs the child will use to sign its DNSKEY RRset, giving the chain Parent DNSKEY --> DS --> Child DNSKEY.

Communication paths vary: direct or API (for example EPP), a web user interface, indirect (email or telephone, common when a third party runs the DNS), or multi-step combinations. The method is aimed at cases where the child and parent are separate. If the parental agent is itself the DNS operator, it can change the delegation directly and does not need this. Some parents want DS records and others want DNSKEY records so they can compute DS themselves; the design works with either.
sections.eli5: The parent keeps a note of which keys the child uses. The child usually has to ask the parent to change that note, and how it asks depends on who runs what.

sections.title: The CDS and CDNSKEY Records
sections.content:
The RFC defines two new resource record types published in the child zone: CDS (Child DS) and CDNSKEY (Child DNSKEY). They convey, from a zone to its parent, the desired contents of the zone's DS record set in the parent. Their wire and presentation formats are identical to DS and DNSKEY respectively, and they use the same registries for their fields. IANA allocated RR code 59 for CDS and 60 for CDNSKEY.

The records express what the child wants the DS RRset to look like after the change. It is a replace operation, and it is up to the consuming software to turn that into adds and deletes and, for CDNSKEY, to generate the DS from the DNSKEY. Authoritative servers and resolvers do no special processing, so for practical purposes these are regular record types. If neither CDS nor CDNSKEY exists in the child, no change is needed.

Use is OPTIONAL. A child that publishes one of the two SHOULD publish both, though it MAY publish only the type its parent consumes. If it publishes both, they MUST match in content.
sections.eli5: The child puts a note in its own records that says here is the list of keys I want my parent to have. The note works like a replacement list, not a list of changes.

sections.title: Acceptance Rules and Parent Behavior
sections.content:
A CDS or CDNSKEY record is accepted only if three rules hold. Location: it MUST be at the child zone apex. Signer: it MUST be signed with a key represented in both the current DNSKEY and DS RRsets, unless the parent uses it for initial enrollment and validates it by other means. Continuity: applying it MUST NOT break the current delegation. If any rule fails, the record MUST be ignored and the error SHOULD be logged.

The parental agent SHOULD use a DNSSEC validator to obtain the records, though it may need a tool that understands these signing rules. The parent MUST choose CDS or CDNSKEY as its default, MAY accept both, and MUST NOT expect both. It can find changes by polling its signed children periodically, or by a user-triggered fetch, and it MAY defer acceptance, for example until the records have stayed in place for some time. If no CDS or CDNSKEY exists, the parent MUST take no action and MUST NOT delete or alter the existing DS RRset.

The agent MUST ensure older versions do not overwrite newer ones, for example by comparing RRSIG signature inception or SOA serial numbers. If the parent calculates the DS itself from CDNSKEY, it can work in a full mode (only DS records it computes) or an augment mode (ensuring DS records for the digest algorithms it requires), and the result may differ from the child's CDS only in digest algorithms.
sections.eli5: The parent only believes the note if it is in the right place, signed with a key it already knows, and wouldn't lock the child out. If there is no note, the parent leaves everything as it is.

sections.title: A Double-DS KSK Rollover
sections.content:
Appendix B walks through a Key Signing Key (KSK) rollover using the Double-DS method from RFC 6781, with key A replaced by key B. The child adds a CDS listing both keys, and after the parent publishes the new DS and the DS TTL passes, the child switches its KSK and signer to B. After the DNSKEY TTL passes the child removes A from its CDS, the parent cleans up its DS set, and the child may finally delete the CDS.

The table's wait steps show which RRset must expire from caches before moving on. Zone Signing Keys are left out because they do not matter in a KSK rollover.
sections.eli5: It is like swapping keys in two steps: first the parent learns about both the old and new key, then the child starts using the new one, and last the old key is forgotten.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Automation only covers the normal case. If a child removes all the DNSKEYs that are in the DS set, it can repair things only by contacting the parent or restoring the keys. If the signing system is compromised, an attacker could publish new CDS or CDNSKEY records and extend the effective time of the attack; a delay in accepting DS changes, as in RFC 5011, gives a chance of detection. A compromise of the registrar account is not mitigated, because the new registrant can change the DS records at will.

The mechanism SHOULD NOT be used for initial enrollment of keys, because there is no way to ensure the first key is the correct one. If it is used, strict rules such as hold-down times and a challenge mechanism MUST be used. A child also cannot use it to go from signed to unsigned, since an empty CDS or CDNSKEY RRset means no change. The mechanism SHOULD NOT be used to bypass intermediaries that cache information, and old data must be allowed to expire from caches before DS or DNSKEY records are deleted.

On the benefit side, third-party DNS providers can maintain DNSSEC information without registrants handing over registrar credentials. The authors also expect that removing humans from the process will reduce DNSSEC-related outages. All information involved is public, as the RFC's privacy section notes.
sections.eli5: The new-key note is a good shortcut but a poor way to start from nothing, because the parent has no way to know the very first key is really the child's. And if a thief gets the child's signing machine, they can leave fake notes.
